questions.q: Why are the language's hooks (such as the iteration method) stored under symbols instead of string names like "iterator"?
questions.explain: Adding a hook under a string name would change the behaviour of every object that happened to have that property. A symbol created by the language cannot collide with anything already written.
options: Symbols are faster to look up than strings
Existing objects might already use any string name for something else; a new symbol is a key no existing code can be using
Strings cannot be used as method names
Symbols are private, so nobody can call the hooks by mistake

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Every Symbol() call creates a new, unique value. The description is only a label for people, and two symbols can share one.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The string key "note" and the symbol stored in note are different keys, so both values live side by side. That is the point of symbol keys.
options: leave at gate | leave at gate

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Object.keys and JSON.stringify skip symbol keys. Reflect.ownKeys returns string and symbol keys, so it sees two.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Object spread copies own enumerable properties, symbol keys included. JSON has no way to represent a symbol key, so it drops it.

questions.q: Is data stored under a symbol key private?
questions.explain: Symbols hide data from ordinary listing tools, not from code that looks for it. For real privacy use #private class fields or closures.
options: Yes: only code with the symbol can ever reach it
No: Object.getOwnPropertySymbols lists the keys, so any code can read it; symbols only prevent accidental clashes
Yes, unless the object is frozen
No, because symbols are converted to strings when used as keys

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Symbol.for returns the same registered symbol for the same name. Symbol() makes a new, unregistered one, so Symbol.keyFor has no name for it.

questions.q: Your app and a plugin load two different versions of the same package. The package checks value[CHARGE] === true, where const CHARGE = Symbol("Charge"). A charge made by one copy is passed to the other. What happens?
questions.explain: Each copy of a module runs its own top-level code, so each gets its own unique symbol. A protocol that must work across copies should use Symbol.for("package.Charge").
options: The check passes, because the descriptions match
The check fails, because each copy created its own Symbol("Charge"), and the two symbols are different keys
The two copies merge into one at runtime

questions.q: Why should registry symbols have namespaced names like Symbol.for("shop.log.redact") rather than Symbol.for("redact")?
questions.explain: Symbol.for gives the same symbol to everyone who asks for the same name. That is the goal within one protocol, and a risk between unrelated ones.
options: Short names are not allowed in the registry
The registry is shared by every library in the process; a short, generic name may already be used by someone else for a different protocol

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Multiplication wants a number. A template literal wants text. Binary + does not know yet whether it will add or join, so it passes "default", even when the other side is a string.

questions.q: Money throws for every hint except "string". What does this print?
questions.explain: The template literal asks with the "string" hint. "Total: " + price uses binary +, whose hint is "default", so the method throws. Use template literals for text.

questions.q: An object has both valueOf and [Symbol.toPrimitive]. What does this print?
questions.explain: When [Symbol.toPrimitive] exists, JavaScript calls it for every conversion and never consults valueOf or toString.

questions.q: Why can valueOf alone not give a money type "text is fine, arithmetic is an error"?
questions.explain: Without a hint, valueOf has to answer every numeric request the same way. Symbol.toPrimitive(hint) knows what the operation wants and can refuse some operations only.
options: valueOf receives no hint, so it cannot tell a template literal from a + b or a * 2

questions.q: Which Symbol.toPrimitive policy fits a Money type best?
questions.explain: Formatted text is always safe to show. A bare number loses the currency, so arithmetic should go through methods like plus that check currencies and fail loudly otherwise.
options: Return the minor units for every hint
Return the formatted text for every hint
Return formatted text for "string"; throw for "number" and "default" and point to explicit methods

questions.q: For a Duration stored in seconds, the lesson allows the "number" hint to return seconds. Why is that fine for durations but not for money?
questions.explain: The right policy depends on whether the number still means the whole value. Seconds do; kobo without "NGN" do not.
options: A number of seconds fully describes a duration, while a bare number of minor units loses the currency
The "number" hint only works for time

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Date has its own Symbol.toPrimitive that treats the "default" hint as "string". Binary + therefore joins text; - asks for a number.
questions.code:
const d = new Date(Date.UTC(2026, 0, 1));
console.log(typeof (d + 0), typeof (d - 0));

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Both calls end up in Object.prototype.toString, which reads the Symbol.toStringTag property to build the label.

questions.q: Can you use Object.prototype.toString.call(value) === "[object Array]" as a security check that value is a real array?
questions.explain: The tag is a label the object provides. It is good for logs and debugging, not for decisions that must not be fooled.
options: Yes, the tag cannot be changed
No: any object can define [Symbol.toStringTag] and claim to be an "Array"; use Array.isArray
Yes, but only in strict mode
No, because arrays have no tag

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A static [Symbol.hasInstance] method replaces the usual prototype-chain check. The plain object has a numeric weightKg, the array does not.
options: TypeError: Shippable is not a constructor

questions.q: What is the main drawback of customising instanceof with Symbol.hasInstance?
questions.explain: It works, but it hides a duck-type check behind an operator with a well-known meaning. Explicit names are easier to read and search for.
options: It is slower than a prototype check
Readers expect instanceof to mean "created by this class"; changing its meaning surprises them, so a plain function like isShippable is clearer

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: #minor in value is true only for objects the class constructor actually initialised. Spread does not copy private fields, and inheriting from a real instance does not give an object its own private field.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Objects declared with using are disposed when the block ends, in reverse order of declaration, like closing nested resources by hand.

questions.q: A function declares using lock = acquire() and then throws. What happens to the lock?
questions.explain: using works like a try/finally written for you: disposal runs however the block ends, and the error continues to the caller afterwards.
options: It stays open, because the function did not finish normally
Its [Symbol.dispose]() method runs as the block is left, before the error reaches the caller
The error is swallowed so that dispose can run
Dispose runs only if the caller catches the error

questions.q: The logger's redaction protocol calls value[redact]() where redact is a symbol. Why not call a method named "redact"?
questions.explain: A protocol keyed by a string could be triggered by accident by ordinary data. In the lesson, a payment's own redact field was logged as plain data because it was not the symbol.
options: String method names cannot return objects
User data can contain a field literally named redact; a symbol key can only be defined on purpose by code that implements the protocol
The logger would have to import every class

questions.q: A class defines [Symbol.for("nodejs.util.inspect.custom")]() to print card numbers masked. Where are the full card numbers still exposed?
questions.explain: A display hook changes what one tool prints. Secrets must be kept out of logged objects, or everything logged must pass through one sanitising function.
options: Nowhere; the hook masks them everywhere
Anywhere that does not use Node's inspect: JSON.stringify, error trackers, database writes, the browser console

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Symbols refuse implicit conversion to text, so "tag: " + tag throws. description is a plain string, and String(tag) also works because it converts on purpose.

questions.q: What does new Symbol("id") do?
questions.explain: Call Symbol("id") without new. Like numbers and strings, symbols are primitive values.
options: Creates a symbol object with the description "id"
Throws a TypeError: symbols are primitives and Symbol is not a constructor

questions.q: Why does the lesson's Money define toJSON() returning { minor, currency } instead of relying on its "string" conversion?
questions.explain: JSON.stringify looks for a toJSON method, then serialises own enumerable string-keyed properties. Store and send exact data; format only for people.
options: JSON.stringify does not use Symbol.toPrimitive; and formatted text like "₦1,500.00" cannot be parsed back reliably, while exact minor units and a code can
Because private fields are always included in JSON

questions.q: Why is the lesson's Money immutable (frozen, with operations returning new objects)?
questions.explain: Objects are shared by reference. A value type such as money is safest when nobody can change it after creation.
options: Prices are shared between carts and orders; if one could be changed in place, a change meant for one cart would affect everything holding that object
So it can be used as a Map key

questions.q: Write markAudited(record, who) that stores who on the record under a symbol key, so it cannot overwrite the record's own auditedBy field and does not appear in JSON.stringify. Also write auditedBy(record) to read it back.
questions.explain: The symbol key sits next to the string key without touching it, and JSON skips it, so the metadata never leaks into API responses.

questions.q: Give Money a [Symbol.toPrimitive](hint) method: for "string" return the amount as NGN 1500.50 (code, a space, the naira value with two decimals); for any other hint throw a TypeError whose message is use plus().
questions.explain: The template literal passes the "string" hint; price + price passes "default", which is refused, so the silent arithmetic becomes a clear error.

questions.q: Make Object.prototype.toString label Booking objects as [object Booking] by adding a Symbol.toStringTag getter.
questions.explain: A getter with the computed name [Symbol.toStringTag] on the class puts the tag on the prototype, shared by every instance.

questions.q: Plugins mark themselves with the registry symbol Symbol.for("shop.plugin"), whose value is the plugin name. Write pluginNames(list) that returns the names of marked objects only. Note that the plugins below create the symbol themselves; you must get the same one.
questions.explain: Symbol.for returns the same symbol for the same name, wherever it is called. The string key "shop.plugin" is a different key, so the fake is ignored.

questions.q: Make Shelf iterable with a generator method under Symbol.iterator, yielding the product names in order, so that spread works.
questions.explain: Spread looks for a method under the well-known symbol Symbol.iterator. A generator method delegating with yield* is the shortest correct implementation, and each spread gets a fresh walk.

questions.q: Finish safeForLog(value): if value is an object with a method under the redact symbol, return what that method returns; if it is a plain object, apply safeForLog to each property value; otherwise return it unchanged.
questions.explain: The protocol check looks for a function under the symbol key. The string field named redact is ordinary data and passes through unchanged.
